headline.s: head to head vs portfolio-v1 (new default)

entries.title: Plan: a portfolio of specialists, picked per kingdom
entries.html:
Steam deals 10 of the 26 cards at random, and a GA genome trained on one fixed kingdom only knows those 10. The new model is a portfolio: about twenty specialists, each evolved with all 26 cards on fresh random kingdoms that always hold its key cards (Witch, Militia, Smithy, Laboratory, Library, Gardens + Workshop, Village + Smithy…), plus a generalist for any kingdom.

The picker is a model too, but not a learned one: when a game starts it plays every specialist on that exact kingdom against the benchmark bots on the C engine (about 25,000 games per second) and the best one plays the game. The new trainer is ga/specialist.py, the model kind ga-portfolio (policy/portfolio.py), and the model goes in its own folder, models/portfolio-v1/.

The nine cards the autopilot can't play on Steam yet (Cellar, Remodel, Library…) are in training. During play they are never bought, and the picker tries each specialist the same way, so it picks one that wins without them. One run, generalist-safe, trains without them as a fallback.

entries.title: A benchmark bug, fixed: every kingdom now gets its own games
entries.html:
The first Witch specialist stalled at the same validation score many times, and the per-bot numbers were suspiciously round (95.0%, 62.5%). The cause: every kingdom in a test set reused the same game seeds. When neither player buys the other kingdom cards, a Witch-and-money deck plays exactly the same game on all 60 kingdoms, so “60 kingdoms × 10 seeds” was really 10 games per seat. The model benchmark (policy.bench) had the same flaw.

Fixed in both: each kingdom gets its own seeds (benchmark version 3), and all models were re-measured. The best old model, k4-20260614, scores 78.9% (it was 81.5%), and k1-steam, the model behind every Steam game so far, scores 43.7%. Those are the numbers to beat. Training restarted with the fix: 21 specialists × 500 generations, about two hours.

entries.title: First two specialists: generalist 71%, Witch 84%
entries.html:
The generalist (any kingdom, all 26 cards) climbed from 59% to 71.2% in 500 generations (5 minutes): 79% against Big Money, 71% against Smithy–Big Money, 63% against Witch–Big Money. For comparison, k1-steam scores 43.7% on random kingdoms.

The Witch specialist reached 83.8% on kingdoms with a Witch (97% / 93% / 60% against the three bots). The best old model, k4-20260614, scores 78.9% on its own Witch kingdoms. Nineteen specialists to go.

entries.title: portfolio-v1 released: 79% on random kingdoms, almost twice k1-steam
entries.html:
All 21 specialists finished (500 generations each, about 5 minutes per specialist). They became one model, models/portfolio-v1/, together with the best old model k4-20260614. It is now the default and the selector's first choice.

Test: 200 random Steam kingdoms the model never saw, 40 games per seat against each fitting bot, played the way the autopilot plays today (the nine blocked cards are never bought):

PlayerScore
portfolio-v1 (picks per kingdom)79.3%

best single specialist (remodel, never buying Remodel)75.7%
k4-20260614 (old best)50.9%
k1-steam (every Steam game so far)41.9%

The pick works: it gets within about two and a half points of a perfect choice and beats every single specialist. With all 26 cards allowed the portfolio would score 80.1%, so teaching the autopilot the nine missing cards is worth about one and a half points overall. The Gardens + Workshop specialist is the clearest case: 87.6% in training but 6.9% without Workshop, so it is never picked today. Workshop is the first card to teach the autopilot.

The stored benchmark (policy.bench) is 75.0%: 87% against Big Money, 74% against Smithy–Big Money, 64% against Witch–Big Money.

entries.title: Every card is playable on Steam now
entries.html:
The nine blocked cards are open. Two halves:

Protocol 2 (the model side): every card's own choices have a request (Cellar, Poacher, Remodel, Workshop, Artisan, Mine, Moneylender, Harbinger, Vassal, Library, Sentry, and Bandit / Bureaucrat when attacked). Each answer is the engine's own decision for that card, asked of the same GA agent that played in training. A test plays 300 engine games and checks, at every card choice, that the answer a player gets equals what the genome did: identical.

The autopilot learned each prompt on the real game, in four games against Very Easy on kingdoms made of the new cards, with a test model that buys them: gains are clicks on the glowing supply pile (Workshop, Remodel, Artisan, Mine), Cellar and Poacher are a hand selection plus OK or Decline, Harbinger and Vassal pick from a pop-up, Library has a Set Aside button, and Sentry needs drag and drop into Trash / Discard / Deck zones. Throne Room had no handler at all before; it does now (Throne Room → Artisan twice works).

Bugs found on the way, all fixed: the “Militia (0 of 2)” counter was read as “discard 0”; a hover tooltip was taken for a discard prompt; the coin count ignored Moneylender, Vassal and Poacher; an unreadable coin counter made a successful Province buy look failed; an empty Estate pile wasn't seen, so Workshop clicked it 58 times; and the GA agent itself kept a Province over a Gold when attacked by Militia (fixed in the Python and C agents).

First real game with all cards: portfolio-v1 against Easy on Gardens, Workshop, Cellar, Remodel, Library, Sentry, Artisan, Harbinger, Vassal, Poacher. The portfolio picked its Gardens + Workshop specialist (98% in its trial on that kingdom, unusable before) and won 34–33. With every card allowed portfolio-v1 scores 80.3% on random kingdoms (79.3% before).

Not yet seen on Steam: the Moat reveal and the Bandit victim's choice (handlers exist). Overnight: round 2 of training, each specialist against the bots and three strong round-1 specialists.

entries.title: Round 2 overnight: specialists that also beat strong opponents
entries.html:
Round 1 trained every specialist against three simple bots. Steam's computer opponents are stronger than those, so round 2 (runs named v2-…) starts from each round-1 specialist and trains it against the bots and a hall of three strong round-1 specialists (generalist, Remodel, Witch). There are six new archetypes too (Workshop, Cellar, Poacher, Vassal, Harbinger, Merchant), and all runs use the fixed agent (Province no longer kept over Gold).

Two measurements, the same for every version: vs bots = the old score on 120 random kingdoms; head to head = the new portfolio and portfolio-v1 each pick their own specialist for a random kingdom and play each other (120 kingdoms × 40 games).

Provisional v2vs botshead to head vs v1
v1 itself (reference)79.2%50.0%
v1 + new pick rule (trial vs bots and the hall)79.1%52.4%
4 of 26 round-2 specialists79.3%53.6%
9 of 26 round-2 specialists79.4%54.6%

Against the bots nothing changes (they are beaten about as well as possible); against strong evolved play the new specialists win more. Example: the round-2 Witch specialist beats the round-1 Witch specialist 66% of the time on Witch kingdoms. A side experiment trains the generalist with four times the budget, to see whether its 71% plateau is the genome's limit.

entries.title: portfolio-v2 released: wins 57% head to head against v1
entries.html:
Round 2 finished overnight: 26 specialists (the 20 archetypes plus Workshop, Cellar, Poacher, Vassal, Harbinger and Merchant), each about 15 minutes, trained against the three bots and the hall of strong round-1 specialists. They form portfolio-v2, the new default, with the pick rule that also tries each specialist against the hall.

200 random Steam kingdomsportfolio-v1portfolio-v2
Head to head (each picks its own specialist)42.9%57.1%
Against the bots80.3%81.0%
Stored benchmark (policy.bench)75.3%76.2%
… against Witch–Big Money63.6%65.7%

What it says: against the simple bots both are near the ceiling, but against strong evolved play the round-2 specialists win clearly more often — the reason to train against the hall. What didn't work: giving the generalist four times the budget (population 128, 1,000 generations) left it at the same score from generation 475 on; its limit is the genome (fixed buy lists per phase), not training time.

Next ideas: a round 3 with round-2 specialists as the hall (a league), and a richer genome for the generalist. Real Steam games with v2 haven't been played yet.

entries.title: Round 3 (a league against round-2 specialists): no further gain so far
entries.html:
Round 3 (v3-…) starts every specialist from its round-2 version and trains it against the bots plus four strong round-2 specialists (generalist, Witch, Gardens, Market). With 8 of 26 done, a provisional portfolio-v3 plays portfolio-v2 50.4% head to head (120 kingdoms) — a tie — and scores 80.2% against the bots, the same as v2. Round 2 gained 7 points head to head; round 3 gains nothing measurable.

Reading: the specialists have reached what their strategy shape can express, the same plateau the generalist hit overnight. portfolio-v2 stays the default; round 3 keeps running and is only released if the full set beats v2.

The next real gain needs a richer genome, not more training. The clearest gap: the agent never looks at the score. It will buy the last Province even when that ends the game in a loss, and it never takes a cheap Duchy or Estate that would end the game while ahead. An endgame rule using both scores (in the Python and C agents together) is the most promising next step; the autopilot would then also need the opponent's score from the screen.

entries.title: Tested and dropped: an endgame rule that looks at the score
entries.html:
The idea from the last entry, built into both agents (Python and C) as a switch so it could be measured cleanly: win now = if a buy ends the game with me ahead, take it; don't end losing = never buy the last Province (or a third empty pile) when that leaves me level or behind.

Each portfolio-v2 specialist played itself with the rule on against the rule off, 6,000 games on random kingdoms: 49.8%. Each half alone: win-now 50.1%, don't-end-losing 49.6%. Against these strategies the score check almost never changes the outcome (they already take Provinces whenever they can), and holding back the last Province mostly hands it to the opponent. So it was reverted: no strength, more complexity, and the autopilot would have needed to read the opponent's score from the screen.

entries.title: Morning experiments: the GA portfolio is saturated
entries.html:
Every cheap way to get more out of the current model was measured head to head (or against the bots where noted):

ExperimentResultKept?
Round 3: league training against round-2 specialists (8 of 26 done)50.4% vs v2still running; released only if it wins
Endgame rule: win now / never end the game losing49.8% vs no ruleno, reverted
Longer pick trial (300 games per opponent instead of 120)80.4% → 81.0% vs botsyes (a few seconds at game start)
Bigger pool: v1 and v2 specialists together (47)50.1% vs v2no
Money gate: no Province before the deck holds enough money50.0% vs no gateno (the evolved lists already wait)
Rollout search prototype (12 simulated futures per buy option)~20% vs no searchno: far too noisy

Reading: the evolved buy lists already contain the simple Dominion heuristics, and selection is within about 2.5 points of a perfect pick. The next real gain needs a different kind of player. The most promising is rollout search done properly: start simulations from the current position in the fast C engine, use the same random futures for every option, and only overrule the specialist when an option wins clearly more often. That would be its own trainer, trainers/search-v1, using the same protocol.
